explain: Problems solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic algorithm. It does not mean 'not polynomial'.

q: Which statement about P and NP is known to be true?
explain: A deterministic algorithm is a nondeterministic one that never uses choice. Whether P = NP is an open problem.

q: What does choice(S) do in a nondeterministic algorithm?
options: Picks an element of S that leads to success, if one exists
Picks a random element of S
Picks the smallest element of S
Tries every element of S in turn
explain: It is an idealised 'lucky guess'. Trying every element in turn is how a deterministic machine has to simulate it.

q: A problem is in NP if, for every 'yes' instance…
options: a certificate exists that can be verified in polynomial time
it can be solved in polynomial time
a certificate can be found in polynomial time
explain: Checking must be fast; finding the certificate may be slow. Solving it in polynomial time would put it in P.

q: Which is the decision version of the travelling salesperson problem?
options: Is there a tour of cost at most k?
Which city should be visited first?
explain: Complexity classes are defined for yes/no questions.

q: Which of these problems is known to be in P?
options: Is there a subset with sum exactly T?
explain: The Euler test only checks degrees and connectivity. The other three are NP-complete.

q: Sorting (as a decision problem, e.g. 'is this array a sorted permutation of that one?') is in NP.
explain: True. It is in P, and P ⊆ NP. Being in NP says nothing about being hard.

q: How long does verifying a subset-sum certificate (a list of indices) take?
explain: Check the indices are distinct and valid, and add up the chosen numbers.

q: The O(n·W) dynamic program shows that the 0/1 knapsack decision problem is in P.
explain: False. W takes only about log W bits to write down, so n·W can be exponential in the input length. The algorithm is pseudo-polynomial.

q: How many branches can a deterministic simulation of n binary choices need to explore?
explain: Each choice doubles the number of possible computation paths.
